extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism, reporters, and general readers interested in the history and practice of American journalism
extracted.subtask_description: A compact historical survey tracing the origin, development, and political power of American journalism, intended to inform students, practitioners, and readers about the press's role in democracy and professional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of opinion / free press
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of opinion is the greatest of all liberties; the free press is essential to democracy and to the exercise of popular sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book repeatedly asserts that freedom of expression (a free press) is fundamental — exemplified by the Zenger acquittal (1734) as 'the dawn of the Revolution.' Historical examples (licensing acts, censorship, pillory, imprisonment) show threats to this liberty and the importance of resisting them. Relevant passages: preface/introduction emphasis on liberty of opinion and Zenger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as maker of public opinion / political power
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers shape citizens' thought, ethics, tastes, and interest in national affairs — they 'make and unmake governments' and must be 'reckoned with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate journalism by its influence on public opinion and political outcomes (extension of suffrage, abolition, revolutionary mobilization). The book treats press impact as a key metric of its historical importance (quoting Rhodes, Godkin, De Tocqueville).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist must be action-oriented and truth-seeking
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism is 'literature in action — action first and action last'; the journalist must first see the truth and not be deceived by lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality journalism prioritizes active pursuit of facts and immediate, effective reporting over purely literary refinement. Even literary journalists (e.g., Dana) succeeded because they were 'men of action.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve democratic reform and minority causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The press should further democratic causes and reforms; many major reforms (e.g., abolition, suffrage expansion) were advanced through journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newspapers by whether and how they mobilize public sentiment for reform and give voice to minorities or progressive causes. Historical examples include abolitionist press and press-driven suffrage efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and teach the historical background of the craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and students must know the background and pedigree of their craft; understanding pioneers and past struggles is essential professional preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends concise historical study for students and practicing reporters; mastery of fundamentals includes knowledge of early printers (Benjamin Harris, Zenger) and institutional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist censorship and government licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism must oppose governmental licensing and censorship; statutory or common-law controls undermine the press's democratic function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book documents licensing acts, licensor figures (L'Estrange), colonial restrictions, and argues these were harmful. A normative criterion for producing journalism is to maintain independence from such restraints and be prepared to face legal consequences for principled publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance commercial motives with political responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial pressures and the need to attract readers coexist with the press's political responsibilities; editors may act for profit yet produce political effects (e.g., Bennett).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating papers, consider both market-driven practices (sensationalism, melodrama) and their civic consequences. The book illustrates trade-offs (Bennett increased readership through sensational methods while also enlarging political engagement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide engaging, locally relevant news to build readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving readers news of events around them promotes interest and participation — newspapers should report the everyday events that connect people to public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bennett and similar editors succeeded by making newspapers relevant to readers' lives. Evaluate content by its ability to engage broad audiences and increase civic awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as watchdog and organizer (mobilizing the public)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key function of the press is to keep citizens informed and organized — to keep 'phalanxes compact' across dispersed communities and thus enable collective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess journalism on its effectiveness in informing, coordinating, and mobilizing public opinion across geographic and social distances (colonial example of using press to unify the thirteen colonies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization and formal training for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism has become a recognized academic and professional career; schools of journalism and training are important for preparing practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality in journalism production is tied to institutional training, professional standards, and awareness of historical/political context. The preface recommends the book for students in journalism schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize political/effective function over literary taste
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging journalism historically or practically, emphasis should be placed on political effectiveness rather than on literary refinement or 'taste.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts editors like Bennett (large political influence despite coarse style) with literary editors (Bryant) to argue that influence and effectiveness can outweigh literary merit in assessing newspapers' historical role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage to publish controversial or unpopular views
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must be willing to risk persecution (imprisonment, pillory) to defend free expression and advance public causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book documents many instances of printers and editors jailed or punished for publication; bravery in the face of legal and social sanction is presented as a normative attribute of influential journalism (e.g., Zenger, colonial printers).
